set.rappels: Do not rappel the East Ridge. Descend the South Ridge line from the three-bolt summit anchor: 4 rappels on a single 60 m rope, one per pitch.
set.rappel_count_note: Counted for one 60 m rope: summit to the pitch-3 bolts, pitch 3 to the big ledge above pitch 2 (the rope comes up about 15 ft short, so downclimb the last bit), pitch 2 to the top of pitch 1, and pitch 1 to the base. Parties with a single 70 m rope usually get down in three rappels with some downclimbing, because it reaches better stances. Do not run one long rappel from the summit to the top of pitch 2: a crack just under the summit bolts and another near the slung boulder at the end of pitch 2 are both known rope-eaters.
set.descent_text: Do not rappel the East Ridge itself: the ridgeline lacks good rappel anchors and is loose and exposed in a way that makes retracing it dangerous. Instead, from the summit, scramble back to the North-South ridge crest and use the South Ridge rappel line from its three-bolt summit anchor. On a single 60 m rope it is four rappels, one per pitch: a short one to the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 3; one toward the big ledge with a slung boulder above pitch 2, which comes up about 15 ft short so you downclimb the last bit; one down pitch 2 to the top of pitch 1; and one to the base. Do not skip from the summit straight to the top of pitch 2 in one long rappel: a crack just below the top anchor is known for jamming ropes. Anchors are a mix of fixed bolts and natural slung-boulder anchors reinforced with webbing, so carry spare tat. From the base, downclimb the class 3-4 gully back to the notch and retrace the approach across the slabs to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass to the trailhead.

rappel_detail.pull: Pull from the ledge with the strands held out from the wall so neither end swings back into the crack under the summit anchor.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 4 on a single 60 m rope: a short rappel from the summit bolts down the uppermost pitch to the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 3.
hazards: A crack a couple of feet below the summit bolts is notorious for wedging rope. Stopping at the pitch-3 ledge instead of running the rope through to the top of pitch 2 is the accepted way to avoid it, and is the single most repeated warning on this descent.
Serpentine is slick rock, and slicker still when damp or dusty; the summit stance is small and the start of the rappel is over the edge rather than off a ledge.
rappel_detail.station: The three-bolt anchor on the serpentine summit block at the top of the climb. The rappel off it is short and awkward — a sit-and-spin start straight off the bolts — and drops the last pitch to a two-bolt station on a narrow ledge at the top of pitch 3. Break here even though the terrain below looks like it would go in one longer rappel.

rappel_detail.pull: This is the crack that eats ropes on this route. Walk the strands well out from the base of the wall before pulling, and pull briskly so the tail does not drop back in behind the boulder.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 4. Knot the rope ends: on a 60 m you run out of rope above the ledge and downclimb the last few metres.
rappel_detail.anchor: two bolts on a narrow ledge, top of pitch 3
hazards: Coming up short leaves the rappeller hanging on a slick serpentine face above the ledge. Knot the ends and confirm the rope reaches before the last person commits.

A crack near the second slung boulder at the end of pitch 2 has wedged a rope end on the pull; the pitch is easy enough that one party simply scrambled back up to free it, but that is luck rather than a plan.
rappel_detail.station: Two bolts on a narrow ledge at the top of pitch 3, replacing older pitons. The rappel aims for the large ledge with a slung boulder near the top of pitch 2. A 60 m rope comes up about 5 m (15 ft) short of that ledge and a 70 m only just makes it, so on a 60 m finish with a short downclimb on Class 3 rock to the ledge.

rappel_detail.pull: This is the crack that eats ropes on this route. Walk the strands well out from the base of the wall before pulling, and pull briskly so the tail does not drop back in behind the boulder.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 3 of 4, down pitch 2 to the anchor at the top of pitch 1.
rappel_detail.anchor: slung boulder and fixed slings on the big ledge above pitch 2
hazards: Slung-boulder and horn anchors are the weakest links on this descent and have been found tattered by arriving parties.

A crack near the second slung boulder at the end of pitch 2 has wedged a rope end on the pull; the pitch is easy enough that one party simply scrambled back up to free it, but that is luck rather than a plan.
rappel_detail.station: Rig from the slung boulder and fixed slings on the big ledge above pitch 2. These are natural anchors reinforced with webbing and are rebuilt periodically, so carry a few metres of spare cord rather than assuming the tat is fresh. On a single 60 m rope, the rappel from here reaches the top of pitch 1.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 4 of 4, to the base. Below it, downclimb the gully back to the notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: anchor at the top of pitch 1 (slung boulder or slings)
hazards: Below the last rappel the gully back down to the notch is class 3-4 and loose, with the approach talus and slabs beneath it.
rappel_detail.station: The anchor at the top of pitch 1. The last rappel lands on the base ledges and the class 3-4 gully where the climb started.

set.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the South Ridge climbing line itself (or, for parties who diverge, the closely parallel Southwest Face). From the summit it is four rappels on a single 60 m rope: (1) a short rappel down the uppermost pitch to a two-bolt anchor on a narrow ledge; (2) a rappel down to a large ledge with a slung boulder near the top of pitch 2, which a 60 m rope reaches only just short, so downclimb the last bit - do not be tempted to skip straight from the summit to the top of pitch 2 in one long rappel, since a crack just below the top anchor is notorious for wedging and stuck ropes have resulted; breaking it at the pitch-3 ledge avoids this; (3) a rappel down pitch 2 to the top of pitch 1; and (4) a final rappel down to the base ledges and gully where the climb started. Anchors are a mix of fixed two-bolt stations and natural slung-boulder/horn anchors reinforced with webbing - carry a few extra feet of tat/webbing since the natural anchors get replaced periodically and can be tired. Below the last rappel, downclimb the class 3-4 gully back to the notch and retrace the approach talus/slabs to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass.

set.rappels: About 20 to 25 chain-station rappels down the Infinite Bliss line, with downclimbing between; no single-rope station list is documented.
set.rappel_count_note: Counts for this rappel line differ, from about 22 to 25. One 60 m rope reaches only about 30 m per rappel, and no source says where a party with one rope would break the longer stations, so a single rope may need intermediate anchors or downclimbing that nobody has described. The alternative to rappelling is to traverse over the mountain and descend the far side, but that terrain is brushy and cliffy and has cost parties an extra night out; rappelling is the advised descent. Budget 3 to 4 hours or more.
set.descent_text: From the summit block reverse the heather benches and downclimb back into the Infinite Bliss line, then rappel the entire route - roughly 20 to 25 chain-station rappels, interspersed with downclimbing. One 60 m rope reaches only about 30 m per rappel and no single-rope station list is documented, so work out each gap before committing. Watch for parties climbing below you; the whole descent runs down a gully-slab that funnels anything you dislodge straight onto them. Budget 3-4 hours minimum for the rappels and start them with enough daylight left — a 2014 fatality on this rappel line happened when a climber skipped a station in fading light and rappelled off unknotted rope ends.

review.single_rope: No single-rope station list found; sources describe chain stations with longer rope setups and 22-25 rappels. A far-side walk-off exists but is reported as brushy and cliffy.
review.changed: Removed the longer-rope setup wording and the claim about 70/80 m single ropes; stated the single-rope unknown plainly; kept the count range, time and safety facts.

set.rappels: Rappel Sisyphus from the treed ledge after pitch 7, or finish the climb and scramble to the top. No single-rope line from below the treed ledge is documented.
set.rappel_count_note: Most parties stop at the treed ledge and rappel Sisyphus. Below that ledge, the rappels are described only for longer rope setups; no source gives a single 60 m rope line or where intermediate anchors would go, so a party with one rope should plan to top out and scramble off instead of bailing from low on the route.

review.single_rope: Not documented below the treed ledge; the single-rope-safe plan is topping out (scramble) or Sisyphus from the ledge.
review.changed: Removed the longer-rope sentence; stated plainly that no single-rope line is known below the treed ledge.

set.rappels: Rappelling the rib itself is not recommended and involves much downclimbing. The standard exit traverses north over the subsummits to one rappel of about 30 m from a slung tree at the middle summit, on a single 60 m rope, then the Southeast Couloir.
set.rappel_count_note: One rappel of about 30 m, within reach of a single 60 m rope. Fixed webbing and a rap ring have been left at this station; inspect them before use.

review.single_rope: The one standard rappel is about 30 m (100 ft), fine on a single 60 m rope; sources note a short rope is enough there.
review.changed: Removed the double-ropes remark about rappelling the rib; kept the existing one-station table and descent text.

set.rappels: The route is descended by rappelling the line of ascent back to the notch. No single-rope count or station list is documented. Anchors are a mix of fixed pitons, bolts, slung horns and nuts of varying age, and some parties have found none at all, so bring slings and cord to back up or build each station.
set.rappel_count_note: The top pitch has been descended on a single-rope rappel, and the last rappel from the first-pitch ledge drops straight to the ground. How many stations lie between, and their lengths, are not documented, so plan on stations short enough for one 60 m rope (about 30 m or less) and downclimb the easy ledges where they are not.
set.descent_text: Descend the route. From the summit, downclimb the easy but exposed top of the ridge to the first anchor and rappel back down the line of ascent, using the ledges on the crest and its west side as stations, until you are back in the notch north of the peak. The stations are a mix of old fixed pitons, bolts, slung horns and nuts, some parties have found no fixed anchors at all, and any tat left there should be inspected and backed up. From the notch, descend the loose scree gully carefully (keep the party close to limit rockfall), and at its foot rejoin the climbers' path and follow it back north to the hairpin pullout on the highway. In mid-September the top pitch was descended on a single-rope rappel, and from the lower ledges a hidden anchor (a nut plus a horn) lies a scramble away, first climber's left then right; the last rappel from the first-pitch ledge drops straight to the ground with no need to traverse.

review.single_rope: Rappel the line of ascent; only the top pitch and the last rappel are described as single-rope; no count or station list found online.
review.changed: Removed the 'carry two ropes' wording from rappels and descent_text; stated what is not known for one rope.
